text.content:
When a spider tries something uncertain — a lock, a sleeping cat, convincing a human the scratching in the wall is nothing — you roll dice. Six-sided dice. Only six-sided dice.

The Core Mechanic

Roll a handful of d6s. Every die showing 5 or 6 is a Success. The Storyteller says how many Successes the task needs. You get them or you don't. That is the entire engine. Everything after this is detail.

The One Rule: Roll your pool of d6s. Count every 5 or 6 as a Success. Get enough and the thing happens. Fall short and it doesn't — and something else goes wrong. The dice do not care about your plan. The dice do not care about anything.

Building Your Dice Pool

Your pool = the relevant Attribute + Skill. The ST tells you which apply. Add them, grab that many d6s, roll.

Example: Pebbles, a Wolf Spider Bruiser, wants to shove a stuck cabinet door. The ST calls for BODY + Athletics. Pebbles has BODY 4 and Athletics 3, so she rolls 7 dice against a Difficulty 3 door. She rolls three Successes and flings the door open hard enough to bounce it off the wall. She succeeded. The heist may not have. The human is awake now.

DifficultySuccessesWhat It Looks Like
Trivial1Crossing an empty counter. Nothing is happening.
Easy2Moving quietly while the TV is on. Picking up a small thing without dropping it.
Moderate3Picking a lock. Sneaking past a drowsy cat. Most of a normal heist.
Hard4Sneaking past an alert cat. Cracking a password. Surviving the exterminator.
Absurd5Stealing a specific item from a locked case while the cat watches and the vacuum is running.

Full Success — it worked. You got enough Successes. The thing happens. Enjoy it. The Alert is still right there.

Partial Success — it worked, but. At least half the Successes you need (round up), but fewer than all of them. You make progress and a complication lands. The lock opens, but you made noise. You clear the gap, but you drop the bag. The ST picks the complication — ideally the funniest one that also actually costs you something. By default it's noise: the Alert rises by 1. The ST may swap that for a complication that costs as much — a dropped item, −1 die on your next roll, a hit from a threat that's engaged — but never both. At Full Alert the noise costs nothing, so a Partial costs a hit from an engaged threat if there is one, otherwise −1 die on your next roll (or the ST's dropped item); in a group check, every Partial pays its own.

Failure — it did not work. Fewer than half the Successes you need (at Difficulty 1–2, zero). No progress, and something gets worse. Failure is a beat, not a wall. The door stays shut and there's a noise now. Every failure should cost something and reveal something. Whenever a rule says you fail a roll, it means this: a Partial is never a failed roll. You may try again next round, and an engaged threat that sees you fail lands a hit (see Vitality) — the one with the biggest attack, if several do. A threat is engaged when it was already active and able to reach you this round, or when you're fighting it; one that only notices you because of this roll isn't engaged yet. If the crew is still stuck after five rounds at one obstacle, the ST ends it: in the heist the objective slips out of reach; in the Escape, anyone still inside is caught.

Critical Success — you did it perfectly. Double the required Successes (6 on a Difficulty 3, 8 on a Difficulty 4). It works better than planned — you get the item and spot a second way out — and the Alert drops by 1 (only on a roll of Difficulty 3 or higher, after every modifier). This is the only thing that lowers the Alert during a heist. Savor it.

Pass or Fail

When a rule only asks whether you pass — “make a Stealth roll or the Alert rises,” “on a success” — a Partial passes and costs nothing extra. An NPC making a check needs the full Difficulty; its roll has no Partial.

The Botch

Your pool has been reduced to 0 or below — by Vitality penalties or a situation so bad the ST rules you can barely function (crushed against a surface, total darkness, upside down in a jar). You still roll one die. On a 1–3, Botch: you fail and the Alert jumps by 2. On a 4–6, a clean failure: an ordinary Failure, no bonus disaster. This time. A Botch die can't be Clutched.

A Botch is what happens when the Bruiser attempts subtlety at Stealth 0 while Critical. Once the table recovers, it is very funny.

Assists

Any crew member in the same scene who isn't the one rolling can Assist, as their Action, if they can actually reach or help the active spider — usually meaning adjacent on the grid, or connected by a silk line, or otherwise plausibly lending a hand. They roll one Skill only — any of theirs that plausibly helps, the ST's call, not necessarily the roller's; no Attribute — to a maximum of 3 dice, minimum 1. Each Success adds one die to the active spider's pool. Only one spider can Assist a given roll. Your Assist is your roll, so you can put your own Silk dice into it (they don't count toward its 3); Silk never goes on a crewmate's roll.

However many helpers and abilities pile in, a roll gains at most +2 bonus dice from Assists, Perks, Signature Moves and intel together. Silk Point dice (Overclock's included) don't count toward that limit.

Group Checks

When the whole crew must get past the same thing — sneak across a room, climb a cabinet, run for the vent — every spider rolls, and each one gets through on its own result. The round raises the Alert only once, by the worst result among those rolls — the largest rise any one of them would have caused — and a Critical lowers it only if every roll was a Critical. Against a creature, it rolls once for the round, and that Difficulty applies to every spider in the check. On a heist obstacle, a group check counts as both of its rolls.

Opposed Rolls

When you act against a creature that's actively resisting — an alert cat, a guard spider, a vacuum in pursuit — it rolls its pool first, and its Successes + 1 become your Difficulty. (A tie still goes to the world; it's bigger than you.) Then every Difficulty modifier applies as usual — cover, the Alert band, Perks, Flaws — and your roll reads Partial, Success or Critical like any other. The creature's roll is just a count: it never Partials, Criticals or Botches. Humans never roll to spot you: you roll against their Chapter 15 Difficulty, as against anything without a stat block. Assists work normally, but only the spider side can receive one.

When Not to Roll

Not everything needs dice. If success is guaranteed, just say yes. A Stealth 4 spider crossing an empty kitchen at 3 a.m. walks across. The same spider crossing while the cat stares directly at it rolls.

Roll when the outcome is uncertain and failure would be interesting. If either is false, skip the dice. The story doesn't need a d6's permission to continue.

One square is about one spider, and every distance is counted in squares. Your Speed comes from your species; diagonal moves count as one square. Hurt halves it (round down); halvings don't stack.

Move + One Action

On your turn you may move up to your Speed and take one Action. You can split your movement — move a few squares, act, move the rest.

An Action is the thing you roll for, or a deliberate equivalent: pick a lock, make a Stealth check, shove a door, spit silk, Assist an ally, patch a crewmate, use a Signature Move (unless it says otherwise). You get one per turn. Sneaking is an Action too, and so is a roll to squeeze or climb under pressure. One roll covers one thing: pick a lock in the cat's sight, and a Failure means it noticed — no extra Stealth roll. Rolls forced on you (a dodge, a shrug-off, a Flaw's check) are free.

Free actions don't cost your Action: a quick word to the crew, dropping an item, glancing around. If you're not sure whether something is free, it probably takes your Action. Free actions and “when…” Perks work on the ST's turn too. A reaction to a roll or an Alert rise — That's Not What Happened, Plausible Deniability, Abort Abort, Damage Control — can be called until the end of that round; the ST undoes what it cancels.

Line of Sight and Cover

Line of sight is a straight line from your square to another that isn't fully blocked by a wall or solid object. Glass blocks silk, not sight: the cat can watch you through the window.

Cover: with a solid object between you and something that might see you, your Stealth Difficulty against it drops by 2, and anything trying to target you rolls at +2 Difficulty.

Climbing, Heights and Squeezing

  • Climbing a wall or ceiling costs normal movement. Slick or hostile surfaces cost double movement, or an Acrobatics roll if the ST calls for one. Rough ground costs +1 movement to enter.
  • Height: crossing somewhere a fall would really hurt adds +1 Difficulty to Acrobatics rolls.
  • Heights are squares too: a chair seat 2, a counter or desk 3, a tall shelf 6, the ceiling 8. Up on a surface, you have cover from anything below. Spiders anchor as they climb, so a failed climb is a slip; a real fall (knocked off, line cut) is a hit of 1 die per 2 squares fallen, rounded up.
  • Squeezing: a gap smaller than a square takes an Acrobatics roll (Difficulty 2), as your Action, to pass — when something is watching or closing in; otherwise it just takes your move. In an Escape obstacle, the obstacle's own roll covers it. Cellar Spiders ignore this entirely.
  • Occupied squares: you can't end your turn in another creature's square. You may pass through an ally's square, not an enemy's — except a Cellar Spider, who folds around anything.

Turn Order

Only when timing is tight: the crew takes its turns first, in any order it agrees on, then the ST runs the threats.
